## What this guide is for

This is an *R* guide that shows how to go from measured vapour pressure vs. temperature
data to the thermodynamic quantities that describe a liquid's
liquid-vapour equilibrium using the Clausius–Clapeyron relation

The overall approach - turn a non-linear physical relationship into
something you can fit a straight line to, then read the physical
quantities off the slope and intercept - is the same one used earlier for temperature-dependent reaction rate constants. Where a step is essentially identical to that earlier case, this guide says so rather than re-explaining it from scratch, so work through that material first
if anything here feels unfamiliar.

Some code below is complete; some has blanks marked `___` for you to
fill in with your own column names, values, or file paths. Basic R
mechanics (assignment, `mutate()`, `filter()`, `lm()`, plotting) are
covered in the introductory R guide and are not re-explained here either.

## Setting up

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(readxl)   # new here - reads Excel files, the same idea as read_csv()
```

## Importing your data

### From your own measurements, recorded in Excel

If you recorded your own readings by hand during a lab exercise, they are
probably sitting in an Excel file rather than a `.csv`. `readxl`'s
`read_excel()` reads a `.xlsx` file straight into a tibble, the same way
`read_csv()` reads a `.csv` - both hand you back a tidy data frame,
`read_excel()` just points at a different file type.

```{r}
#| eval: false
vapour_data <- read_excel("_______")   # fill in your file's path/name
```

#### Structuring your spreadsheet so it imports cleanly

`read_excel()` works best when the sheet underneath is already tidy, meaning one
variable per column, one measurement per row. A few habits make the difference:

- Start the table in the top-left corner: the first header in cell `A1`,
  the data filling out from there. `read_excel()` begins reading at the
  first non-empty cell.
- Give every column a single, plain header in the first row.
- Put the unit in the header, not in the cells. A column headed `T_C`
  holding bare numbers (`17.5`) imports as a number you can compute with;
  the same readings typed as `"17.5 C"` import as text and have to be
  cleaned up first. 
- Keep one variable per column: a `T_C` column and a separate
  `p_mano_mbar` column, not both crammed together.
- If you measured more than one substance, give it its own column (e.g.
  `liquid`) rather than using a separate sheet, or the sheet's name, to
  say which substance a block of rows belongs to.

A tidy version of the same data might look like this, with `liquid` sitting
in cell `A1`:

| liquid   | T_C  | p_mano_mbar |
|----------|------|-------------|
| Liquid A | 17.5 | -490        |
| Liquid A | 15.0 | -545        |
| Liquid B | 17.5 | -564        |
| Liquid B | 15.0 | -612        |

Laid out this way, every column is exactly one variable, every row is exactly one
measurement, and `read_excel()` (or `read_csv()`) can hand it back to you
with no cleanup needed.

### From a larger provided csv dataset

If instead you've been given a ready-made dataset as a `.csv` file  import it the way you already know using `read_csv()`.

The same tidy layout applies either way: whatever the file type, you
want one row per measurement and one column per variable before moving
on.

## (If applicable) Correcting raw instrument readings

The manometer reading is not the vapour pressure yet: it is measured
against the zero point ("nulpunktet"), the reading taken with the
container evacuated before any liquid is added. Subtract that zero point
to get the real pressure. Define it once near the top of your script,
with a comment giving its meaning and unit, then correct the column in
its own `mutate()` step before anything else:

```{r}
#| eval: false
p_zero_mbar <- ___   # manometer zero point, mbar - substitute your own value

vapour_data <- vapour_data %>%
  mutate(p_real_mbar = p_mano_mbar - p_zero_mbar)  
```

If your pressure column is already the true vapour pressure, skip this
step and work directly with the column you were given.

## The Clausius-Clapeyron relationship

The Clausius-Clapeyron equation relates a liquid's vapour pressure to its
temperature and its enthalpy of vaporisation. Integrated between a
reference state and the state you measure, it can be written as

$$
\ln \left( \frac{p}{p_0} \right) = -\frac{\Delta_{vap}H}{R} \cdot \frac{1}{T} + \frac{\Delta_{vap}S}{R}
$$

- $p$: the vapour pressure at temperature $T$
- $p_0$: the standard pressure, $1\ \text{bar} = 1000\ \text{mbar}$
- $\Delta_{vap}H$: the enthalpy of vaporisation
- $\Delta_{vap}S$: the entropy of vaporisation
- $R$: the gas constant, $8.314\ \text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
- $T$: the absolute temperature, in Kelvin

If this looks like the linearised Arrhenius equation from earlier in the
course, that's because the underlying move is identical: a quantity that
depends exponentially on `1/T` becomes, after taking its natural log, a straight
line in `1/T` whose slope and intercept are used to determine the physical constants you
want. 

### Setting up the linearisation

Same as the Arrhenius linearisation: add the line's two axes as columns -
`inv_T` (`1 / T_K`, with `T_K` in Kelvin) for x, and `ln_p`
(`log(p / p0)`) for y.

```{r}
#| eval: false
p0_mbar <- 1000   # standard pressure, 1 bar, in the same unit as your p column

vapour_data <- vapour_data %>%
  mutate(
    T_K   = ___,    # your temperature column, converted to Kelvin
    inv_T = ___,    # 1 / T_K
    ln_p  = ___     # natural log of (your pressure column / p0_mbar)
  )
```

## Fitting a line per substance

With more than one liquid in the same data frame, fit each one
separately - the same pattern already covered for handling several
conditions in the same dataset earlier in the course: check the exact
category values, then `filter()` to one substance and pass that straight
into `lm()`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
unique(vapour_data$liquid)   # check the exact spelling of each substance
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
lm_A <- lm(___ ~ ___, data = filter(___))
# add one more lm() line per substance, following the same pattern
```
Make sure to name each `lm()` object something that makes sense for the substance it fits.

Visualise all of them on one plot by mapping `color` to `liquid` *inside*
`aes()` - a mapping, so each substance gets its own points and its own
fitted line, with a legend added automatically:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(vapour_data, aes(x = ___, y = ___, color = ___)) +   # linearised axes; colour by substance
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "___", y = "___", color = "___") +   # your own axis and legend labels
  theme_classic()
```

For more on styling your plots, see the section at the end of this guide.

## Collecting the results in one tibble

Rather than juggling separate `slope_A`, `intercept_A`, `slope_B`,
`intercept_B`, ... variables, it's much easier to gather one row per
substance into a single tibble, then compute everything else with
`mutate()` on that tibble directly. Here it is worked through concretely
for two made-up substances and fitted models (substitute your own `lm()`
objects and substance names):

```{r}
#| eval: false
vapour_results <- tibble(
  liquid    = c("Liquid A", "Liquid B"),
  slope     = c(coef(lm_A)[[2]], coef(lm_B)[[2]]),
  intercept = c(coef(lm_A)[[1]], coef(lm_B)[[1]]),
  r2        = c(summary(lm_A)$r.squared, summary(lm_B)$r.squared)
)

vapour_results
```

Add one more entry to each of `liquid`, `slope`, `intercept` and `r2` per
extra substance if you have more than two.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A tidier alternative, for reference
`group_by(liquid)` + `summarise()` fits one line per substance in a single
step, so you don't write a separate `lm()` call for each. It fits the
model once per group, keeps it in a `model` column, and pulls the slope,
intercept and R² out of it with the same `coef()` and `summary()` you'd
use on a single `lm()`. If the `lm()`/`coef()`/`summary()` calls are
unfamiliar, see the [linear regression
reference](https://cpdse-edux.github.io/R_documentation/topics/linear-regression.html).

```r
vapour_results <- vapour_data %>%
  group_by(liquid) %>%
  summarise(
    model     = list(lm(ln_p ~ inv_T, data = pick(everything()))),
    intercept = coef(model[[1]])[[1]],
    slope     = coef(model[[1]])[[2]],
    r2        = summary(model[[1]])$r.squared
  ) %>%
  select(-model)
```

Same result as the tibble above, just scaling to any number of
substances without adding a line per substance by hand.
:::

## Reporting the fitted line and R² on your figure

A figure showing a fitted line is more useful with its equation and R² values reported somewhere - either directly on the plot, or written into the figure's caption. Which you use is mostly a matter of preference (and how many lines are on the same plot). For reporting directly on the plot, a guide can be found [here](https://cpdse-edux.github.io/R_documentation/topics/linear-regression.html). Alternatively, report the fitted line and R² in the figure caption rather than on the plot itself. Record the slope, intercept and R² from the results data frame and add to your caption (e.g. *"The fitted line for Liquid A is y = 1.23 - 4567x, R² = 0.987."*)

## From slope and intercept to $\Delta_{vap}H$ and $\Delta_{vap}S$

Comparing the linearised equation above to a straight line
`y = slope * x + intercept` shows what the fitted numbers mean:
the slope is $-\Delta_{vap}H / R$ and the intercept is $\Delta_{vap}S / R$. Rearrange and add both as new columns on
the results tibble:

```{r}
#| eval: false
R_gas <- 8.314   # J / (mol K)

vapour_results <- vapour_results %>%
  mutate(
    DvapH_kJmol = ____,   # kJ/mol
    DvapS_JKmol = ____    # J / (K mol)
  )
```

## Standard and normal boiling points

Two different "boiling points" are worth distinguishing here, and both
are read off the same fitted line, just in different ways.

The **standard boiling point** i.e. when `p = p0` (1 bar = 1000 mbar) is the temperature where the line crosses `ln(p/p0) = 0`. Rerrange the linearised Clausius-Clapeyron equation to determine the standard boiling point from $\Delta_{vap}H$ and $\Delta_{vap}S$.

The **normal boiling point** is the temperature where `p` reaches normal
atmospheric pressure (1 atm = 1013 mbar). This is the mirror image of
extrapolating a fitted line to a new condition, covered earlier in the
course: instead of reading a `y` value off the line at a known `x`, you
solve `y = slope * x + intercept` for `x` at a known `y`.

```{r}
#| eval: false
p_atm_mbar <- 1013
ln_p_normal <- log(p_atm_mbar / p0_mbar)   # the "y" you're solving for x at

vapour_results <- vapour_results %>%
  mutate(
    Tb_standard_K = ___,   # the standard boiling point in Kelvin
    Tb_standard_C = ___,   # convert standard boiling point to Celsius 
    inv_T_normal  = ___,   # solving y = slope*x + intercept for x, when p = 1 atm
    Tb_normal_K   = ___,   # convert inverse temperature (1/T)
    Tb_normal_C   = ___    # convert normal boiling point to Celsius
  )

```

## Exporting your results

`select()` the columns that actually belong in a report - the helper
columns (`slope`, `intercept`, `inv_T_normal`, and so on) were only
needed to get there. You can also deselect them with `select(-slope, -intercept, ...)` if you prefer.

```{r}
#| eval: false
vapour_results_final <- vapour_results %>%
  select(____)

vapour_results_final
```

You can export the results to different file formats. `write_csv()` writes a `.csv`, the exact
reverse of `read_csv()`. `write_xlsx()` (requires the `writexl` package) writes an `.xlsx` if you
would rather open it in Excel. Use whichever suits you.

```{r}
#| eval: false
write_csv(vapour_results_final, "vapour_pressure_results.csv")

library(writexl)   # install once with install.packages("writexl")
write_xlsx(vapour_results_final, "vapour_pressure_results.xlsx")
```

A figure can be saved the same way with `ggsave()`, which by default
saves whichever plot was drawn most recently:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggsave("vapour_pressure_plot.png", width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 300)
```


## Tips for styling your plots

Here are some optional tips for making your figures more readable and
professional.

### Point size

The default size of points in `geom_point()` is often a bit small for a
report figure. Adjust it with `size` (experiment with different
numbers):

```{r}
#| eval: false
geom_point(size = ____)
```

### General text size

Most themes (e.g. `theme_classic()`) take a `base_size` argument that
scales all text in the figure (axis titles, legend, etc.) at once:

```{r}
#| eval: false
theme_classic(base_size = ____)
```

### Math in axis titles

Plain text in `labs()` can't correctly show fractions, subscripts,
superscripts or Greek letters, which the axis titles in this analysis all
need - `1/T`, `ln(p/p0)`, units like `K⁻¹`. Use `expression()` instead:

```{r}
#| eval: false
labs(
  x = expression(1 / T ~ (K^{-1})),   # 1/T axis, unit K^-1
  y = expression(ln(p / p[0]))        # ln(p/p0) axis
)
```

A few building blocks you can combine inside `expression()`, using this
analysis as the examples:

- `x[number]` makes a subscript, e.g. `p[0]` → p₀ for the reference
  pressure.
- `x^{number}` makes a superscript, e.g. `K^{-1}` → K⁻¹, or
  `J~K^{-1}~mol^{-1}` → J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ for the units on $\Delta_{vap}S$.
- `frac(a, b)` draws an actual fraction, e.g. `frac(1, T)` → $\frac{1}{T}$
  stacked rather than a slash.
- Greek letters are written by their English name, e.g. `Delta`, and
  combine with a subscript for `Delta[vap] * H` → $\Delta_{vap}H$.
- `degree` draws the ° symbol, e.g. `expression(T ~ (degree * C))` → T (°C).
- `~` inserts a small space between parts; `*` joins them with no space.
- Plain text needs to be in quotes - anything else can be interpreted as
  a mathematical symbol or variable name.

### Adjust axis limits

Set `limits` to fix the axes, and `expand = c(0, 0)` to remove the
automatic "padding" ggplot otherwise adds around the data.

`limits` takes `c(min, max)` in the data's own units. Pick a range that comfortably
contains all your points; anything falling outside the limits is dropped
from the plot.

```{r}
#| eval: false
scale_x_continuous(limits = c(____, ____), expand = c(0, 0)) +
scale_y_continuous(limits = c(____, ____), expand = c(0, 0))
```

> **Note:** with `expand = c(0, 0)`, points sitting right in a corner are
> often half cut off by the edge of the figure. Try adding
> `coord_cartesian(clip = "off")` if that happens.

### Regression lines that extend beyond the data points

`geom_smooth()` by default only draws the line between the lowest and
highest data point. `fullrange = TRUE` instead asks it to extend across
the whole range of the axis **scale**:

```{r}
#| eval: false
geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, fullrange = TRUE)
```

> **Tip:** `fullrange = TRUE` only extends as far as the axis scale itself — so it only has a visible effect if that range goes beyond your data, e.g. via `scale_x_continuous(limits = c(___, ___))`. Without wider `limits`, the line just spans the data as usual.

### Shape and color together - combine into one legend

`shape` works just like `color`, but gives each group its own point
shape (circle, triangle, cross) instead of a color - useful for
colour-blind readers, and because colors often disappear in
black-and-white printing. Add it in the same place as `color`, inside
`aes()`.

If you map `color` and `shape` to the **same** variable, ggplot
automatically merges the two legends into one instead of showing two
separate ones - this makes the figure less cluttered and easier to read:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ggplot(data, aes(x = ____, y = ____, color = ___, shape = ____)) +
  geom_point() +
  labs(color = "____", shape = "____")   # same title in both places -> merges into one legend
```

> **Note:** the title in `labs()` must be identical for `color` and
> `shape` (literally the same text string), or the two legends stay
> separate.
